clue.text: For tireless worker, job at last — engaged by leader for tests

indicators.note: something engaged by another is held or occupied by it, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: Joe Root captained England's Test cricket side

indicators.note: at last points to the final letter of the word job

explanation.surface: A cricket captain takes on one final job for a tireless helper.
explanation.walkthrough: Joe Root was England's Test cricket captain, so the 'leader for tests' is ROOT; it engages B, the last letter of 'job'. 'For' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: A robot is a machine that works without ever getting tired.

clue.text: You shouldn't have to stand being transported in this

definitions.text: You shouldn't have to stand being transported in this

parts.words: You shouldn't have to stand being transported in this
parts.note: 'stand' sounds like putting up with something, but means standing up on a train or bus

explanation.surface: A complaint about something you should not have to tolerate while being carried away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stand' and 'transported' suggest enduring rapture; they mean standing in a vehicle.
explanation.definitionFit: A booked place on a train or coach guarantees you a place to sit.

clue.text: British have nowhere to swim here?

definitions.text: British have nowhere to swim here?

parts.note: to lack a pool is to have nowhere to swim

explanation.surface: A wry question about a British seaside resort with nowhere to swim.
explanation.walkthrough: Blackpool is a classic English seaside resort in Lancashire, so the joke is that it lacks a pool.
explanation.definitionFit: The Lancashire resort is somewhere Britons famously go for a dip, so the question is ironic.

clue.text: Open venue, or not, as may be

indicators.note: suggests the letters could fall in any order, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: A place that may or may not host the Open.
explanation.walkthrough: The Open is golf's British championship; Royal Troon in Scotland is one of its rotating courses.
explanation.definitionFit: This Ayrshire golf course regularly hosts the Open Championship.

clue.text: A perfect term of French

parts.note: the French phrase for exactly the right word, borrowed into English

explanation.surface: A grammar note about the French perfect tense.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Perfect term' reads like a grammar tense or school term, but it means the ideal word, and the phrase for that is itself French.
explanation.definitionFit: The borrowed French expression means precisely the right word or phrase for the purpose.

clue.text: I met adult, badly disfigured

indicators.note: badly signals the letters are mangled into a different order

explanation.surface: Someone recalls meeting a grown-up who had been terribly scarred.
explanation.definitionFit: Something mutilated has been severely damaged or deformed, so disfigured is a synonym.

clue.text: You must have support of course, when husband intrudes

indicators.note: something that intrudes pushes into the middle of another, so it goes inside

parts.note: a tee supports the ball on a golf course

explanation.surface: Reassurance that you will naturally be backed up when your husband barges in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Of course' looks like 'naturally'; it means on a golf course, where a tee supports the ball.
explanation.definitionFit: Thee is the old object form of the second-person pronoun.

clue.text: Unaided, people replacing one are still wrong

indicators.note: replacing means one piece is swapped out and another put in its place

parts.note: one is the Roman numeral I
men means people

explanation.surface: Without help, staff who replaced someone are still making mistakes.
explanation.definitionFit: A text left unamended has had no corrections, so its errors remain.

clue.text: Giant moon, one missed by artist

indicators.note: something missed by another is left out of it, so these letters are removed

parts.note: Titian was the Venetian Renaissance painter
one is the Roman numeral I

explanation.surface: A painter failing to see a huge moon.
explanation.definitionFit: Saturn's largest satellite bears this name, and it is one of the biggest moons in the solar system.

clue.text: Past hates often reviewed as instinctive

indicators.note: looked at again in a new way, so the letters of these words are rearranged

explanation.surface: Old grudges, when reconsidered, turn out to be gut reactions.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something by the seat of the pants means acting on instinct and feel rather than plan.

clue.text: Newly licensed, eats food here?

indicators.note: newly means made afresh, so these letters are arranged anew

explanation.surface: A recently licensed shop where you can buy something to eat.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue does double duty: the anagram, and a description of a shop selling prepared food.
explanation.definitionFit: A deli sells cooked meats, cheeses and other ready-to-eat food.

clue.text: Arouse new enthusiasm about reader

parts.note: re means about or concerning
the Kindle is Amazon's e-book reader

explanation.surface: An e-book reader that revives someone's love of books.
explanation.definitionFit: To rekindle interest is to stir it up again, figuratively relighting a fire.

clue.text: News of people passed on in a meeting like this

definitions.text: News of people passed on in a meeting like this

parts.words: News of people passed on in a meeting like this
parts.note: 'passed on' suggests gossip relayed, but means the dead, whose messages a medium claims to receive

explanation.surface: Gossip about people circulated at a meeting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Passed on' looks like news being relayed; here it means people who have died.
explanation.definitionFit: At a spiritualist sitting, a medium claims to bring messages from the dead.

clue.text: Stretches, so elegant when dancing

indicators.note: dancing letters move about, so the letters of these words are rearranged

explanation.surface: A dancer stretches out, looking so graceful.
explanation.definitionFit: To elongate something is to lengthen it, so it is a synonym of stretches as a verb.

clue.text: Bar supporters: it would be unfair to move them

definitions.meaning: the uprights hold up the crossbar on a football pitch

definitions.text: it would be unfair to move them
definitions.meaning: moving these is the idiom for changing the rules mid-contest

explanation.definitionFit: The posts hold the crossbar, and shifting them is the idiom for unfairly changing the rules.

clue.text: Church official's bag is brown, full of rupees

indicators.note: full of means the other letters contain this one

parts.note: a sac is a bag or pouch
tan is a light brown

explanation.surface: A clergyman's satchel is a brown one stuffed with Indian money.
explanation.definitionFit: This officer of a church looks after the sacred vessels and vestments.

clue.text: Put name to excellent port

parts.note: to dub something is to give it a name
A1 means first-rate; the figure 1 is written as the letter I

explanation.surface: Signing off on a fine wine of the fortified kind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Port' could be the wine; it is the harbour city on the Persian Gulf.
explanation.definitionFit: Dubai is a major harbour city of the United Arab Emirates.

clue.text: Directors here said to be fed up with the place

indicators.note: points to a word spoken aloud that sounds like another

parts.note: bored means fed up
a room is a place or space

explanation.surface: The directors are reportedly sick of where they meet.
explanation.definitionFit: Company directors hold their meetings in the room named after their board.

clue.text: Saucy dance by girl with sex appeal

parts.note: Sal is a girl's name, short for Sally

explanation.surface: A cheeky dance performed by a sexy young woman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Saucy' looks like cheeky, but it hints the word is also a sauce.
explanation.definitionFit: This Latin dance shares its name with a spicy Mexican sauce, hence a dance that is saucy.

clue.text: In TV show, play with the facts

definitions.text: In TV show, play with the facts

parts.words: In TV show, play with the facts
parts.note: 'play with the facts' sounds like distorting truth, but means a drama built on real events

explanation.surface: A television programme that takes liberties with the truth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Play with' suggests tampering; read 'play' as a noun, a drama containing real facts.
explanation.definitionFit: A dramatised documentary is a television play reconstructing actual events.

clue.text: Plea to move work back into war-torn city

indicators.note: letters moved around are rearranged into a new order
back means the abbreviation for work is read backwards

parts.note: op, short for opus, is a work

explanation.surface: An appeal to send a project back into a city ravaged by war.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plea to move' reads as a request to relocate, but 'to move' is the anagram signal giving ALEP, and 'back' reverses the abbreviation for opus.
explanation.definitionFit: This Syrian city was devastated by fighting during the civil war.

clue.text: Little pictures, each meaningful or just interesting on first inspection

indicators.note: looking only at the start of each word picks out its opening letter

explanation.surface: A comment that small images may seem significant or merely curious at a glance.
explanation.definitionFit: These tiny icons in text messages are small images expressing ideas or feelings.

clue.text: Shift left, after one's settled in Kansas City

indicators.note: something settled in a place sits inside it, so these letters go within the city

parts.note: Dodge City is a Wild West town in Kansas

indicators.note: after places the letter for left behind the letters for one's

parts.note: one's read as 'I is', giving IS

explanation.surface: Someone moves out of the way after making a home in Kansas City, Missouri.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Kansas City' wants to be the Missouri city; it is Dodge City, Kansas. ISL goes inside DODGE.
explanation.definitionFit: To dislodge something is to force it out of position, so shift as a verb.

clue.text: Parasite caught in part of foot when getting up

indicators.note: the clue word that signals this step
in a down entry, getting up means the word is read from the bottom upwards

parts.note: the heel is part of the foot
C is the cricket abbreviation for caught

explanation.surface: A bloodsucker catches hold of someone's heel as they rise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' is the insertion signal: C goes inside LEEH, the heel turned upside down.
explanation.definitionFit: This worm attaches itself to a host and feeds on blood.

clue.text: Successfully deal with catch on end of line

parts.note: to cop is to catch

indicators.note: end of picks out the last letter of the word line

explanation.surface: An angler lands a fish at the end of the fishing line.
explanation.definitionFit: To cope with something is to manage or handle it successfully.

clue.text: But it is usually adults who benefit from this nepotism

definitions.text: But it is usually adults who benefit from this nepotism

parts.words: But it is usually adults who benefit from this nepotism
parts.note: the phrase for favours handed to friends names boys, yet the friends are grown men

explanation.surface: A grumble that grown-ups are the real winners from favouritism.
explanation.walkthrough: The idiom for handing posts to cronies mentions boys, which the clue plays against the adults who actually benefit.
explanation.definitionFit: This British idiom describes giving positions to friends or allies rather than on merit.

clue.text: In teens, I fancied I was a genius

indicators.note: fancied means imagined or made up, so these letters are made into something new

explanation.surface: An adult remembers believing in adolescence that they were brilliant.
explanation.definitionFit: The physicist's name is used as a byword for anyone of extraordinary intellect.

clue.text: Restrict severely, being in the minority

indicators.note: in shows the answer is found inside the words that follow

explanation.surface: Clamping down hard on a small group.
explanation.definitionFit: To hem someone in is to surround and confine them, limiting their freedom tightly.
